title: Joel Becker: Reconciling Impressive AI Benchmark Performance, Limited Developer Productivity Impacts
summary: METR's Joel Becker contrasts exponential time-horizon benchmark growth with the 2025 developer RCT slowdown, explains why the gap exists, and says newer uplift data is unreliable but likely shows speedup.

assertions.quote: they take 20% longer to complete tasks when they're allowed to use AI versus not.

verdicts.note: Accurately reports METR's July 2025 RCT (16 devs, ~19% slower); the finding is specific to that setting and early-2025 tools.

assertions.quote: they say that AI made them complete tasks in 20% less time.

verdicts.note: METR found devs believed they were ~20% faster while measured slower; other studies also show self-reports outrunning measured gains.

assertions.quote: plotted with log log scaled y- axis, it looks remarkably steady um in its exponential pattern.

verdicts.note: METR's 2025 time-horizon study found ~7-month doubling (faster in 2024-25); later measurements stayed on or above trend, with wide error bars.

assertions.quote: in the recent past, it looks like it's um it's accelerating or or or rising rising more quickly.

verdicts.note: METR noted a faster ~4-month doubling for 2024-25 models; later data roughly held, though the sample is small and uncertain.

assertions.quote: about half of the cases that Sweetbench measures as um as as passing these algorithmic tests would be merged into Maine by these maintainers.

verdicts.note: METR's own analysis and follow-ups found many benchmark-passing patches aren't mergeable; messy, high-context work lags benchmark scores.

assertions.quote: maybe you need 99% reliability at the one hour um time horizon to get uh to get speed up on on task an hour

verdicts.note: A reasonable explanation consistent with METR's 44% acceptance and review overhead; the specific threshold is conjecture.

assertions.quote: these developers are very highly familiar with their work and that these repositories are large and complex.

verdicts.note: Consistent across Stanford's data, METR's mature-repo slowdown and long-context degradation results.

assertions.quote: I think this is sort of significantly understating the degree to which people are sped up today.

verdicts.note: Newer models may help, but METR attributed much of the slowdown to context, review overhead and repo familiarity, not model quality alone; METR's own later follow-up was mixed.

assertions.quote: developers who expect to be sped up very significantly are systematically dropping out of our data.

verdicts.note: METR's Feb 2026 update reported this selection problem; how much it biases estimates is uncertain.

METR Feb 2026: more developers declined to join because they won't work without AI, and 30-50% withheld tasks they didn't want to do without AI. METR calls its estimate a likely lower bound and is redesigning the study (pay cut from $150 to $50/h also contributed).

assertions.quote: speed up can can greatly overstate the the degree to which people are getting more value out of AI.

verdicts.note: Speedup on cheap tasks need not translate into value, but AI can also enable new valuable work, so the direction is case-dependent.

The 56% lab speedup would imply nearly twice as many tasks, but real-world field experiments measured only a 26% increase in completed tasks, showing lab task speedups overstate on-the-job gains (though gains remain positive).

METR Feb 2026: developers changed task types and output quality (tests, docs) under AI, so time differences 'may not represent value-differences'. This gap can run in either direction; METR itself thinks its estimate understates uplift.

A doubling of completeness came with a measurable loss in comprehension (-5.95 pp), and the tasks where AI helped most (D4) showed the steepest loss (55% vs 93% correct). The authors argue downstream costs may offset the time saved, but they did not measure those costs.

assertions.quote: They enjoy using cursor more as a as a sort of um workflow

verdicts.note: Consistent with METR's perception gap and surveys reporting less frustration/fatigue; a plausible explanation rather than a measured mechanism.
